3. Who You're Actually Reaching

Reach isn't the problem. Who that reach is landing on is worth a closer look.

Full audience breakdown from one of your reels — followers vs non-followers, and the complete age split.

85.3% of your viewers are non-followers. That's genuinely good news: Instagram is pushing your content out to new people, which is exactly what you want. The problem sits at the next step — of all those new people, almost none convert into a follow, which is why Section 2's growth line is flat. The age split is right for your audience. This matters because it rules out the easiest excuse. You're not reaching teenagers, you're not reaching the wrong country, and you're not stuck inside a follower bubble. Instagram is putting you in front of the correct demographic at scale and they're leaving in the first three seconds. Every fix in this audit is about that gap, not about reach.

4. The Core Finding

Pulled from retention data across every reel of yours reviewed, regardless of topic, length, or account.

Every video loses 70–86% of your audience in the first 2–3 seconds.

That's the symptom, not the diagnosis yet. Reach isn't the problem — 78–85% of the viewers on your posts are non-followers, mostly served through the Reels tab and Feed. The algorithm is putting your content in front of new people fine. Two things could be causing them to leave, and this audit is built to test both: (1) the account's opening seconds and format — covered below and in Sections 5–10 — and (2) the account's settings and distribution status, reviewed in Section 3. Both are addressed below.

5. Content Craft Check

Six specific, fixable issues sit underneath the retention numbers.

  • 01
    Runtime doesn't match attention. Your longer posts (27s, 31s, 45s) all show the same shape: a steep drop in the first 2–3 seconds, then a long, flat, near-zero tail.
  • 02
    No repeatable format. Every post you've put out is a one-off — different structure, different pacing, a different opening each time. There's no consistent shape your audience learns to recognise, which also means there's no format for you to iterate on.
  • 03
    Your bio does less work than it could. RAF Estates' bio — "Buy·Sell·Rent, Homes, Apartments & Investments" — could describe almost any agent in Dubai. Your personal bio is sharper: "UAE Property Investment Specialist," "serious investors," with a direct "Book a call" CTA. The account growing 3x faster is the one with the sharper positioning — yours.
  • 04
    Your first two seconds say nothing. Across your last three posts, the pattern repeats: cut to a slide, render or property layout, then pan to you opening with "so this is… so this is…" — no claim, no stat, no reason to keep watching. Josh Packer does the opposite: a bold statement or rhetorical hook lands inside the same two seconds, camera already on him.
  • 05
    Your on-screen captions are see-through.
  • 06
    The editing style needs to change. A brief for the editor as much as for you:
    • Solid black-and-white captions instead of see-through text
    • Far less panning at the start
    • More impactful recording — closer framing, facing the camera

Case Study 2 — Mehroz Bhirea

The market right now: August prices fell 1.7% YoY to AED 1,636/sqft — the first annual dip since Feb 2021. Off-plan is 68–70% of sales. AED 10M+ deals rose to 193 in August from 149 in June. By late May, cuts totalled AED 2.36bn across 3,292 properties, with off-plan resales sitting 10–15% below original prices.

Inference, not a sourced fact

Buyers look anxious about timing and off-plan risk right now — content that answers that directly should land harder than generic listing tours.

Five angles worth testing alongside Section 10's formats:

  • What AED X buys you

    "AED 1.5M in Dubai right now — here's five very different lives." Safest format, works on both platforms.

  • Area face-off

Send your own top-10 TikTok/Reels search and this section gets replaced with real observations.

Carousel formats, adapted for RAF Estates

Not every post needs to be a video. Carousels keep people swiping, which Instagram reads as a strong signal, and they're far quicker to produce than a site visit. Three formats that are working right now, reworked for your context:

Traveling iconA small icon that moves across every slide, pulling the eye to the next one.
Follow the lineA single line that runs across all the slides, so the carousel reads as one continuous piece.
Swipe to zoomEach slide zooms further into the same image, so swiping feels like moving closer.

  • Traveling icon → "Your AED 3M, slide by slide"

    A small gold key or pin icon travels across every slide: "Here's what AED 3M gets you in Dubai right now…" → slide 2, a JVC apartment → slide 3, a KBS City townhouse → slide 4, an Al Marjan Island unit → final slide, "DM us 'BUDGET' and tell us yours." The "What AED X buys you" format from above, in carousel form.

  • Follow the line → "The off-plan payment journey"

    One line runs the full width of the carousel, with a stop on each slide: 5% booking → 5% at six months → construction milestones → handover → first rental income. It answers the anxiety about off-plan timing and risk flagged in the market data above, and it's highly saveable, which the algorithm rewards.

  • Swipe to zoom → "From the map to your front door"

    Slide 1: the UAE. Slide 2: Sharjah. Slide 3: Khalid Bin Sultan City. Slide 4: the specific plot. Slide 5: the villa itself, with price and CTA. It builds a curiosity gap one swipe at a time — the viewer keeps going to see where it lands.

The mattk_dxb result: Khalid ran full production — ideation, scripting, filming direction, editing — for a JBR/Marina specialist who only had to film footage once every two weeks. Result: 1 million "niche" organic views and qualified followers, including one video that hit 100,000 views in 24 hours. This is the first of several agents Khalid's worked with — more case studies get added here as those profiles come through.

His 3-pillar structure: every agent he runs this for gets the same three content pillars — teaching people about the community, creating broad and exciting ideas, and talking about what's new in the community. Your content currently has no pillar structure at all; it's one-off posts with no throughline connecting them.

Proven hook formats (across posts with 1M+ views): controversial statements, personal-take "yapper" pieces, ranking videos, comparisons, day-in-a-life, whiteboard explainers, pen-and-screen property breakdowns, POV format, storytelling, and fake-podcast interviews. Each is a repeatable shape, not a one-off idea — the same discipline behind the 12-second format proposed in Section 10. Here's a first pass at what each could look like on your account, built around your investor audience:

  • Controversial

    "Why buying off-plan without checking this one clause could cost you six figures" — a claim serious investors stop scrolling for.

  • Yapper

    Straight-to-camera opinion, no production polish needed: "Everyone's saying the market's slowing down — here's why they're wrong."

  • Ranking

    "The 5 areas serious investors are quietly buying into right now" — a countdown people watch to the end to see if their pick made it.

  • Comparison

    Rental yield or entry price: Dubai vs. Abu Dhabi vs. a market your investor audience is already comparing you against.

  • Day in a life

    A real day — a viewing, a client call, a closing — framed as "what a UAE property investment specialist's day actually looks like."

  • Whiteboard

    Walk through how a payment plan or ROI calculation actually works — exactly the kind of thing "serious investors" in your bio want explained plainly.

  • Pen-and-screen

    Pull up a real masterplan or listing and mark up the specific reason it's worth — or isn't worth — an investor's attention.

  • POV

    "POV: you're viewing an off-plan unit before it's released to the public" — puts the viewer in the investor's seat, not yours.

  • Storytelling

    A real client story — an investor who nearly missed a deal, or one that paid off — told as a narrative, not a listing pitch.

  • Fake podcast

    A sit-down with a colleague or past client on where the market's heading — borrows the credibility of a long interview in short-form time.

These are starting points based on what's in this audit already — if you can share which properties, price points, or investor types you're actively working with right now, these can be turned into specific scripts rather than formats.

Sub-case study — Matt Kaye (@mattk_dxb)

Associate Director, Allsopp & Allsopp · JBR, Dubai Marina & Off Plan · 3,322 followers · 218 posts · AED 400m+ sold

This is the agent from the 1M-view result above, seen up close. His views run roughly 3,000–6,000 with outliers as high as 104K — and looking at what he actually does, three things stand out that apply directly to you:

  • A repeatable hook, not a repeatable format

    He opens with "Hi, good afternoon" or "Good morning and good..." on video after video. As a hook it isn't clever — but it's consistent, and that's the point. His audience recognises him before they've read a word. You don't need a better line than his; you need one you use every time.

  • He builds a curiosity gap in the first frame

    "Difference between the two Five Luxe towers" — with both towers behind him and arrows pointing at them. You don't know the answer, so you keep watching. That's the whole mechanic: a rhetorical question or a statement that opens a loop the viewer needs closed.

  • He shows the subject within 3–5 seconds

    Even when he opens on himself, the camera pans to what he's actually talking about almost immediately. Contrast that with your current pattern — a slide, a sound effect, then "so this is…" at second three, by which point the viewer still doesn't know what they're looking at.

The repeatable hook"Hi, afternoon" — same opening, every video. Recognisable on sight.
Curiosity gap in frame one"Difference between the two Five Luxe towers" — subject on screen, arrows pointing, question open.
Same hook, different setting"Good morning and good..." — the consistency is the asset, not the wording.

The one thing to take from Matt Kaye

A curiosity gap is what stops the retention curve falling off a cliff at second three. You don't need better production than you already have — you need the viewer to have an unanswered question in their head before they've decided whether to scroll. A rhetorical question, a comparison, a claim they want to argue with: any of those work. "So this is…" opens nothing.

This isn't theoretical — it's already been briefed.

The Hook → Context → Body → CTA caption structure below has already been sent to your team directly and applied to a live post ("Start the video with a great hook"). This audit is formalising and extending a fix that's already partially in motion, not proposing something untested.

10. Building a Repeatable Format

The single highest-leverage fix for you — everything else compounds on top of this.

Five hook options to A/B test against each other, not one format to guess is right. Same 12-second skeleton every time — hook (0–2s), visual proof (2–8s), one differentiator (8–11s), same CTA card (11–12s) — only the opening line changes. Post all five, see which two or three actually hold attention, then that becomes the next round of five variants on the winners.

Option 1 — Straight number (the safe default)
Say
"AED 3.2 million. Four bedrooms plus maid's room. That's rare." — price and the specific thing that makes it rare, both in the first line.
Draws on
The base format already agreed — no walk-in, no "so this is," straight to the number.

Say
"Everyone's telling you to buy in Khalifa Bin Sultan City. Here's why I'm not." — a stance people stop to argue with, then you justify it in the visual-proof beat.
Draws on
Khalid's "Controversial" format from Section 5.

Say
"Three reasons Al Marjan Island is the one serious investors are watching right now — number one:" — countdown structure, viewer stays to see all three.
Draws on
Khalid's "Ranking" format from Section 5.

Say
"Same budget, two options: Al Marjan Island or Khalifa Bin Sultan City. Here's what you actually get for your money in each." — forces the viewer to pick a side, which means finishing the video.

Khalid's "Comparison" format from Section 5.

Pull up the actual masterplan on screen, point at it: "This one plot is the reason I'd buy here over anywhere else on Al Marjan Island." — hook and visual proof land in the same second, the way Josh's pen-screen posts do.
Draws on
Khalid's "Pen-and-screen" format from Section 5.

Run all five over your next 10–15 posts, tracking skip rate against the 70–86% baseline from Section 4. Whichever two or three come out ahead become the format you lock in — and the next five variants get built on what's actually working for you, not guessed at again.

Test solid block text over see-through

Your on-screen text sits semi-transparent over the footage. Against a plain wall it's fine; against anything busy it becomes work to read, and a viewer deciding in under a second doesn't do work. Every benchmark account in this audit uses solid, high-contrast text — Mehroz uses white block capitals with a hard shadow, Josh uses bold white-and-blue with an outline, Matt Kaye uses solid white with a dark edge.

Worth testing, not assuming

Run your next batch with solid white block text on a dark strip or with a hard outline, and compare skip rate against your current see-through style on similar posts. The benchmark accounts all landed on solid text independently, which is decent evidence — but your own numbers will settle it faster than copying them will.

12. Cover Images & Thumbnails

Your in-feed hook decides whether someone keeps watching. Your cover decides whether someone browsing your profile taps in at all.

How your grid has changed over time

Earlier: face + one wordYour face on almost every tile, with a single word underneath — "costs", "penthouse", "1 million". Recognisably you, but the word is small and thin, and on its own it doesn't tell anyone what the video is about.
Now: renders, no faceMostly aerial shots and developer renders, very little text, and you appear in one tile out of twelve. At grid size it reads like a developer's brochure — nothing says who you are or why to tap.

The best stretch of your grid is the one covered in Section 6 — your face plus a bold, readable headline on every tile ("How do you transfer funds from UK to Dubai", "Price has doubled in 2 years"). That's also where some of your strongest view counts sit. The current grid has moved away from both of those things at once.

How the benchmark accounts' grids read

Josh PackerHis face on nearly every tile, bold white-and-blue headline on each. Instantly recognisable as one person, one style.
Mehroz BhireaA mix of his face and project renders — but almost every tile carries bold text naming the project or the deal.
Mo MarstaniSame sit-down setting and framing on every tile. Less text, but total consistency — you know it's his before you read anything.
Ryan BoothFace-first, selfie-style, often in the car. Low production, but a person in every frame.
Matt KayeFace plus location — the towers, the view, the area he's talking about, with him in shot.

The pattern: a face or a readable headline on every tile — usually both.

Every benchmark account passes one simple test at grid size: can you tell who this is, or what this video is about, without tapping? Your older grids pass. Your current grid mostly doesn't.

Four cover formats to test

Same principle as the five hook options in Section 10 — run all four, compare, keep the winners. Track taps from profile visits and views per post against your current baseline.

  • Format A — Bold price poster

    Huge yellow, red and white type leading with the number: "AED 4.3M for a standalone 4-bedroom villa", "4 bedroom villa + maid's room for under AED 3.2M. That's rare." Readable at thumbnail size, price-first, and the closest match to what Mehroz and Josh do. Why test it: it's the cover version of the "straight number" hook — the most proven format in this audit, carried onto the grid.

  • Format B — Curiosity-gap question

    "Considering Abu Dhabi?" — a direct question in bold yellow, developer logos, a single strong visual. Why test it: it opens a curiosity gap before anyone has tapped, which is exactly what the in-feed hook has to do too. If a question pulls more taps than a price, that tells you something about what your audience responds to.

  • Format C — Premium editorial

    Refined serif type, restrained colour, the RAF Estates mark: "Standalone Villas with Bespoke Design", "Wadeem Gardens — prices from AED 8.7M". Why test it: your audience is 76% aged 25–44 and investment-focused (Section 3). A premium look may build more trust with that buyer than a loud one, even if it stops fewer casual scrollers. This is the test that tells you whether brand polish or scroll-stopping matters more for your leads.

  • Format D — Face + readable headline

    Your face, front and centre, with a short bold headline across the bottom — "WATCH BEFORE YOU MOVE TO DUBAI", white and yellow with one word in red, UAE flag behind. Why test it: it copies the one pattern every benchmark account shares — a person and a readable headline on every tile. Formats A–C lead with the property; this one leads with you. If Section 1 is right that people follow a person before a brand, this is the format that should win.

Format A — Bold price posterPrice and unit type as the headline, features in icons below, direct CTA.
Format A — Bold price poster"AED 4.3M" in yellow at the top — the number is the first thing the eye lands on.
Format B — Curiosity-gap questionThe question does the work; logos and a map give it credibility.
Format C — Premium editorialSerif headline, clean render, restrained palette — reads as high-end.
Format C — Premium editorialPrice and payment terms presented like a brochure page, RAF Estates branded.
Format D — Face + headlineYour face, the flag, and a four-word headline you can read at grid size. The benchmark formula, in your own style.

Where to start

If you only test two, run Format A against Format D — property-first against person-first. That single comparison tells you more about what your audience responds to than anything else in this section.

13. Roadmap

What changes for you, and when — from this week through the next year.

IMMEDIATE — THIS WEEK

Fix what costs you nothing to fix

None of this needs new content, more budget, or more of your time on camera — it's five changes you (or Atul, on the edit side) can make directly to what's already live.

  • Rewrite the RAF Estates bio. Right now it reads like any agent in Dubai. Pull the specificity from your own personal bio — named specialism, named audience ("serious investors"), one direct CTA — onto the brand account too, so both wrappers carry the same sharp positioning.
  • Trim the following list. A brand account following more people than follow it back reads as inactive or new, even when it isn't — a quick credibility fix with zero content cost.
  • Post the 5 format options from Section 6 — not trialling alongside everything else, but the only thing you post this month, so we get a clean read on which ones actually work.
  • Fix your opening line specifically. Drop "so this is…" and replace it with a claim, a number, or a question inside the first two seconds. This is already half-started — the Hook → Context → Body → CTA caption structure has been sent to your team and used on one post already. This week is about making it the rule, not the exception.
  • Pin one proof post. A closed deal or testimonial, built the way Josh builds his — hard number, your face, your name. Zero content cost, immediate credibility fix. See Section 4.
0–3 MONTHS

Prove the format actually works for you

A fixed format only tells you anything if you run it enough times to see a real pattern rather than one lucky post. This phase is about discipline more than creativity.

  • Post 10–15 videos across the 5 format options from Section 10, no other formats mixed in. Track skip rate on each one against your current 70–86% baseline — the options that pull that number down are the ones that stay.
  • Split what goes where, rather than posting everything to both. Right now every post is a collaboration, so the two accounts are effectively one. The change: property-specific content (listings, walkthroughs, project breakdowns) stays as a collaboration across both accounts, exactly as now. Everything else — market takes, day-in-the-life, client stories, opinion pieces — goes to your personal account only. That gives the personal account its own reason to exist beyond mirroring RAF Estates, and it's the content type that builds the personal brand the numbers already say is working. Every benchmark in Section 7 is a named person, not an agency logo.
  • Split long videos rather than cutting them. Your longer videos exist because your clients need that information — cutting a two-minute walkthrough to 15 seconds loses genuine value, and that's not what this recommends. Instead, break one long walkthrough into several short ones: one on the kitchen, one on the appliances, one on the layout. Same total information, same filming session, but each clip gets its own hook and its own first two seconds. Mo Marstani proves the middle ground works — his informative content runs around a minute, not two to three.
3–6 MONTHS

Add a second format once the first one's proven

Once the 12-second listing format has a track record behind it, this is where the Khalid-style formats from Section 8 come in — not to replace the listing format, but to sit alongside it as a second shape your audience recognises.

  • Introduce a "results" format — closed deals, testimonials, a client story — following Josh's proof-led pattern, but in your own voice rather than copied from his.
  • Start a pinned highlights strip (results / testimonials / more results) the way Khalid structures his own profile — this expands the single pinned proof post from Section 7 into a full rotating set, once you've got more results to show off.
  • Review retention data monthly. If skip rate hasn't meaningfully improved by this point, the format itself needs revising before you add any more volume — don't scale something that isn't working yet.
6–12 MONTHS

Scale what's actually proven for you

This is the only phase where posting more is the right move — and only because, by now, you'll have the data to know it's worth doing rather than a hunch.

  • Increase posting frequency only once the fixed format is consistently beating your current baseline — not before.
  • Consider a signature hook style just for you — the way Khalid's entire account is built around one positioning line. You already have "UAE Property Investment Specialist" as a foundation; this is about making it instantly recognisable in the first frame, every time, not just in your bio.
  • Revisit the two-account structure. Decide whether RAF Estates stays as a parallel brand presence or folds fully behind your personal account — based on which one is actually converting by this point, not on which one "should" in theory.

14. Next Steps

What to build and track from here, so this audit turns into a working system rather than a document.

1. A content calendar

The single most useful thing to create next. It doesn't need to be complicated — a spreadsheet with a row per post and these columns:

  • Post date & account

    RAF Estates collaboration, or personal-only — following the split set out in the roadmap.

  • Format option used

    Which of the five hook options from Section 10 this post is testing. Without this column you can't tell which format won.

  • Hook line

    The actual words in the first two seconds, written before filming, not after.

  • Community / topic

    Which area or project — so clips from one shoot stay linked and the pillar structure holds.

  • Caption CTA keyword

    The word you're asking people to DM or comment, so you know which keyword actually pulls.

  • Caption style

    See-through or solid block, for the test in Section 11.

2. A results tracker

Same sheet, filled in a week after each post goes live. These are the only numbers worth recording:

MetricWhy it mattersTarget
Skip rateThe core problem this audit is solvingBelow the 70–86% baseline, trending down
ViewsReach, for context2,500+ per post, one in ten hitting 10K
Saves & sharesReportedly ranked above likes by the algorithmAny upward movement
Follows from postThe conversion Section 2 shows is currently flatAnything above the current near-zero
DMs / comments with the CTA keywordThe only metric that maps to actual leadsTrack from zero — this is the real scoreboard

3. A monthly review cycle

Once a month, with the tracker open: which two or three format options pulled skip rate down, which didn't, and what replaces the losers. That's the A/B cycle from Section 10 turned into a routine rather than a good intention.

4. Scriptwriting — including re-hooks

Every video gets a short script before it's filmed: the hook line, the three or four points it covers, and the CTA. Not a word-for-word script — a structure, so you walk in knowing the first two seconds and never default to "so this is…".

The hook gets someone to stay past second three. A re-hook keeps them past second ten — a line mid-video that reopens the curiosity gap just as attention starts to dip. Your longer walkthroughs especially need these. A few, adapted for your content:

Re-hookWhat it sounds like in a RAF Estates video
Tease what's coming"Wait until you see the view from the master bedroom."
Reveal a number"Only 361 of these are being released in phase one."
Challenge them"Can you spot the one thing most buyers miss in this floor plan?"
Hold back the answer"Before I tell you the price, look at what's included."
Add a problem"But there's one thing about this community nobody mentions."
Make a comparison"Same budget in Dubai Hills gets you half this space."
Raise the stakes"And the payment plan is where it gets even better."
Warn them"Don't sign an off-plan contract before you check this."
Switch the shotCut from you talking to the view, the kitchen, the plot map — a visual reset every 3–5 seconds.
Call back to the hook"Remember I said AED 3.2M? Here's why that's rare."

Two or three re-hooks in a 30–60 second video is plenty. Write them into the script at the points where the retention curve usually drops.

5. A hook bank

A running list of hook lines that worked — yours, plus ones worth stealing from the benchmark accounts — sorted by mechanic: curiosity gap, specific number, contrarian claim, mistake call-out, hyperlocal reference. When it's time to film you pull from the bank instead of starting from a blank page, which is what causes "so this is…" in the first place.

The one habit that makes all of this work

Write the hook before you film, not after. Every problem in this audit — the flat retention curve, the see-through captions, the missing curiosity gap — traces back to the hook being an afterthought. Decide the first two seconds first, and the rest of the video has something to serve.
